Matrix elements of operators between angular-momentum states turn up everywhere in quantum mechanics: in transition rates, in selection rules, in the energy shifts caused by a magnetic field. Most of them look like hard integrals. The Wigner–Eckart theorem says that for a large class of operators, the tensor operators, almost all of that work is unnecessary. Every matrix element is a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient, which depends only on the angular-momentum labels and can be looked up, times one “reduced” number that doesn’t depend on the magnetic quantum numbers at all.

This memo defines tensor operators and works through the position vector r\vec rr as an example, including the slightly fiddly business of putting it into standard form. Then it proves the theorem, by a construction that the two worked examples after it carry out in full.

1Tensor operators

Throughout, the Ja,J_a\text{,}Ja​, for a=1,2,3,a=1,2,3\text{,}a=1,2,3, satisfy [Ja,Jb]=iεabcJc,[J_a,J_b]=i\varepsilon_{abc}J_c\text{,}[Ja​,Jb​]=iεabc​Jc​, and

J±≡12(J1±iJ2),[J3,J±]=±J±,[J+,J−]=J3,J^\pm \equiv \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\big(J_1\pm iJ_2\big),\qquad [J_3,J^\pm]=\pm J^\pm,\qquad [J^+,J^-]=J_3 ,J±≡2​1​(J1​±iJ2​),[J3​,J±]=±J±,[J+,J−]=J3​,
(1)

as in memo 3. Ja(s)J_a^{(s)}Ja(s)​ denotes the standard spin-sss matrices of memo 3. These are (2s+1)×(2s+1)(2s{+}1)\times(2s{+}1)(2s+1)×(2s+1) matrices with rows and columns labeled by l=s,s−1,…,−s,l=s,s-1,\dots,-s\text{,}l=s,s−1,…,−s, and

[J3(s)]l′l=l δl′l,[J±(s)]l′l=Cs,l± δl′,l±1,\big[J_3^{(s)}\big]_{l'l} = l\,\delta_{l'l},\qquad \big[J^{\pm(s)}\big]_{l'l} = C^\pm_{s,l}\,\delta_{l',l\pm1},[J3(s)​]l′l​=lδl′l​,[J±(s)]l′l​=Cs,l±​δl′,l±1​,
(2)

where

Cs,l±≡12(s∓l)(s±l+1).C^\pm_{s,l} \equiv \frac1{\sqrt2}\sqrt{(s\mp l)(s\pm l+1)} .Cs,l±​≡2​1​(s∓l)(s±l+1)​.
(3)

Equivalently, Ja∣s,l⟩=∣s,l′⟩[Ja(s)]l′l,J_a\ket{s,l}=\ket{s,l'}\big[J_a^{(s)}\big]_{l'l}\text{,}Ja​∣s,l⟩=∣s,l′⟩[Ja(s)​]l′l​, with the repeated index summed.

A set of 2s+12s+12s+1 operators Ols,O^s_l\text{,}Ols​, with l=s,s−1,…,−s,l=s,s-1,\dots,-s\text{,}l=s,s−1,…,−s, is called a spin-sss tensor operator if

[Ja,Ols]=Ol′s[Ja(s)]l′lfor all a,l.[J_a,O^s_l] = O^s_{l'}\big[J_a^{(s)}\big]_{l'l}\qquad\text{for all }a,l.[Ja​,Ols​]=Ol′s​[Ja(s)​]l′l​for all a,l.
(4)

In words: commuting JaJ_aJa​ with OlsO^s_lOls​ gives a linear combination of Oss,…,O−ssO^s_s,\dots,O^s_{-s}Oss​,…,O−ss​ whose coefficients are the lllth column of the spin-sss matrix of Ja.J_a\text{.}Ja​. For example,

[J1,Ols]=[J1(s)]s,l Oss+[J1(s)]s−1,l Os−1s+⋯+[J1(s)]−s,l O−ss.[J_1,O^s_l] = \big[J_1^{(s)}\big]_{s,l}\,O^s_{s} + \big[J_1^{(s)}\big]_{s-1,l}\,O^s_{s-1} + \cdots + \big[J_1^{(s)}\big]_{-s,l}\,O^s_{-s}.[J1​,Ols​]=[J1(s)​]s,l​Oss​+[J1(s)​]s−1,l​Os−1s​+⋯+[J1(s)​]−s,l​O−ss​.
(5)

This is exactly the rule by which the basis states ∣s,l⟩\ket{s,l}∣s,l⟩ transform under Ja,J_a\text{,}Ja​, with “act on a state” replaced by “commute with an operator.” That parallel is the whole content of the Wigner–Eckart theorem.

Remark: Why columns rather than rows? Apply the definition twice: [Ja,[Jb,Ols]]=[Ja,Ol′s][Jb(s)]l′l=Ol′′s[Ja(s)Jb(s)]l′′l.[J_a,[J_b,O^s_l]] = [J_a,O^s_{l'}]\big[J_b^{(s)}\big]_{l'l} = O^s_{l''}\big[J_a^{(s)}J_b^{(s)} \big]_{l''l}\text{.}[Ja​,[Jb​,Ols​]]=[Ja​,Ol′s​][Jb(s)​]l′l​=Ol′′s​[Ja(s)​Jb(s)​]l′′l​. With the Jacobi identity,

[[Ja,Jb],Ols]=[Ja,[Jb,Ols]]−[Jb,[Ja,Ols]]=Ol′s[Ja(s),Jb(s)]l′l=iεabc Ol′s[Jc(s)]l′l=iεabc [Jc,Ols],\begin{aligned} \big[[J_a,J_b],O^s_l\big] &= [J_a,[J_b,O^s_l]]-[J_b,[J_a,O^s_l]] = O^s_{l'}\big[J_a^{(s)},J_b^{(s)}\big]_{l'l}\\ &= i\varepsilon_{abc}\,O^s_{l'}\big[J_c^{(s)}\big]_{l'l} = i\varepsilon_{abc}\,[J_c,O^s_l], \end{aligned}[[Ja​,Jb​],Ols​]​=[Ja​,[Jb​,Ols​]]−[Jb​,[Ja​,Ols​]]=Ol′s​[Ja(s)​,Jb(s)​]l′l​=iεabc​Ol′s​[Jc(s)​]l′l​=iεabc​[Jc​,Ols​],​
(6)

as it must be. With rows instead, [Ja,Ol]=[Ja(s)]ll′Ol′,[J_a,O_l]=[J_a^{(s)}]_{ll'}O_{l'}\text{,}[Ja​,Ol​]=[Ja(s)​]ll′​Ol′​, the same calculation gives the product of the matrices in the opposite order, and the commutator comes out with the wrong sign. The column convention is the one that’s compatible with the algebra. ♣\clubsuit♣

so [J±,Ols][J^\pm,O^s_l][J±,Ols​] has weight l±1,l\pm1\text{,}l±1, and must be proportional to Ol±1s.O^s_{l\pm1}\text{.}Ol±1s​. The constant isn’t free. 3Is r\vec rr a tensor operator?

To find out, we need the commutators [Ja,rb],[J_a,r_b]\text{,}[Ja​,rb​], and for those we need a representation of the JaJ_aJa​ that acts on the same space as r.\vec r\text{.}r. The natural one is the orbital angular momentum,

Ja=εabc rbpc,[ra,pb]=iδab,[ra,rb]=[pa,pb]=0.J_a = \varepsilon_{abc}\,r_bp_c,\qquad [r_a,p_b]=i\delta_{ab},\qquad [r_a,r_b]=[p_a,p_b]=0 .Ja​=εabc​rb​pc​,[ra​,pb​]=iδab​,[ra​,rb​]=[pa​,pb​]=0.
(10)

Let’s confirm that this really satisfies [Ja,Jb]=iεabcJc.[J_a,J_b]=i\varepsilon_{abc}J_c\text{.}[Ja​,Jb​]=iεabc​Jc​. We’ll need the identity

[AB,CD]=A[B,C]D+AC[B,D]+[A,C]DB+C[A,D]B,[AB,CD]=A[B,C]D+AC[B,D]+[A,C]DB+C[A,D]B,[AB,CD]=A[B,C]D+AC[B,D]+[A,C]DB+C[A,D]B,
(11)

which you can check by expanding. For [rdpe, rfpg],[r_dp_e,\,r_fp_g]\text{,}[rd​pe​,rf​pg​], only the first and last terms survive, since the rrr’s commute with each other and so do the ppp’s:

[rdpe, rfpg]=rd[pe,rf]pg+rf[rd,pg]pe=−iδef rdpg+iδdg rfpe.\begin{aligned} [r_dp_e,\,r_fp_g] &= r_d[p_e,r_f]p_g + r_f[r_d,p_g]p_e\\ &= -i\delta_{ef}\,r_dp_g + i\delta_{dg}\,r_fp_e . \end{aligned}[rd​pe​,rf​pg​]​=rd​[pe​,rf​]pg​+rf​[rd​,pg​]pe​=−iδef​rd​pg​+iδdg​rf​pe​.​
(12)

Hence

[Ja,Jb]=εadeεbfg [rdpe, rfpg]=−i εadeεbeg rdpg+i εadeεbfd rfpe.\begin{aligned} [J_a,J_b] &= \varepsilon_{ade}\varepsilon_{bfg}\,[r_dp_e,\,r_fp_g]\\ &= -i\,\varepsilon_{ade}\varepsilon_{beg}\,r_dp_g + i\,\varepsilon_{ade}\varepsilon_{bfd}\,r_fp_e . \end{aligned}[Ja​,Jb​]​=εade​εbfg​[rd​pe​,rf​pg​]=−iεade​εbeg​rd​pg​+iεade​εbfd​rf​pe​.​
(13)

Now cycle the indices of each ε\varepsilonε so that the summed index comes first, and use εkijεklm=δilδjm−δimδjl:\varepsilon_{kij}\varepsilon_{klm}=\delta_{il}\delta_{jm}-\delta_{im}\delta_{jl}\text{:}εkij​εklm​=δil​δjm​−δim​δjl​:

εadeεbeg=εeadεegb=δagδdb−δabδdg,εadeεbfd=εdeaεdbf=δebδaf−δefδab.\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{ade}\varepsilon_{beg} = \varepsilon_{ead}\varepsilon_{egb} &= \delta_{ag}\delta_{db}-\delta_{ab}\delta_{dg},\\ \varepsilon_{ade}\varepsilon_{bfd} = \varepsilon_{dea}\varepsilon_{dbf} &= \delta_{eb}\delta_{af}-\delta_{ef}\delta_{ab}. \end{aligned}εade​εbeg​=εead​εegb​εade​εbfd​=εdea​εdbf​​=δag​δdb​−δab​δdg​,=δeb​δaf​−δef​δab​.​
(14)

So the two terms are −i(rbpa−δab rdpd)-i\big(r_bp_a - \delta_{ab}\,r_dp_d\big)−i(rb​pa​−δab​rd​pd​) and +i(rapb−δab repe).+i\big(r_ap_b - \delta_{ab}\,r_ep_e\big)\text{.}+i(ra​pb​−δab​re​pe​). The two δab\delta_{ab}δab​ terms are both r⋅p,\vec r\cdot\vec p\text{,}r⋅p, with r\vec rr to the left of p,\vec p\text{,}p, so they cancel exactly, leaving

[Ja,Jb]=i(rapb−rbpa).[J_a,J_b] = i\big(r_ap_b - r_bp_a\big).[Ja​,Jb​]=i(ra​pb​−rb​pa​).
(15)

Finally, εcabJc=εcabεcde rdpe=(δadδbe−δaeδbd) rdpe=rapb−rbpa,\varepsilon_{cab}J_c = \varepsilon_{cab}\varepsilon_{cde}\,r_dp_e = (\delta_{ad}\delta_{be}-\delta_{ae}\delta_{bd})\,r_dp_e = r_ap_b-r_bp_a\text{,}εcab​Jc​=εcab​εcde​rd​pe​=(δad​δbe​−δae​δbd​)rd​pe​=ra​pb​−rb​pa​, so

[Ja,Jb]=iεcabJc=iεabcJc,[J_a,J_b] = i\varepsilon_{cab}J_c = i\varepsilon_{abc}J_c ,[Ja​,Jb​]=iεcab​Jc​=iεabc​Jc​,
(16)

and Ja=εabcrbpcJ_a=\varepsilon_{abc}r_bp_cJa​=εabc​rb​pc​ is a valid representation of the algebra.

4The commutator [Ja,rb][J_a,r_b][Ja​,rb​] and the adjoint representation

Since rbr_brb​ and rcr_crc​ commute,

[Ja,rb]=εacd [rcpd, rb]=εacd rc[pd,rb]=εacd rc(−iδdb)=−iεacb rc=iεabc rc.\begin{aligned} [J_a,r_b] &= \varepsilon_{acd}\,[r_cp_d,\,r_b] = \varepsilon_{acd}\,r_c[p_d,r_b]\\ &= \varepsilon_{acd}\,r_c(-i\delta_{db}) = -i\varepsilon_{acb}\,r_c = i\varepsilon_{abc}\,r_c . \end{aligned}[Ja​,rb​]​=εacd​[rc​pd​,rb​]=εacd​rc​[pd​,rb​]=εacd​rc​(−iδdb​)=−iεacb​rc​=iεabc​rc​.​
(17)

Recall the adjoint representation of memo 2, [Jaadj]bc≡−iεabc;\big[J_a^{\mathrm{adj}}\big]_{bc}\equiv -i\varepsilon_{abc}\text{;}[Jaadj​]bc​≡−iεabc​; these 3×33\times33×3 matrices satisfy the algebra. Since −iεacb=[Jaadj]cb,-i\varepsilon_{acb}=\big[J_a^{\mathrm{adj}}\big]_{cb}\text{,}−iεacb​=[Jaadj​]cb​,

[Ja,rb]=rc[Jaadj]cb.[J_a,r_b] = r_c\big[J_a^{\mathrm{adj}}\big]_{cb}.[Ja​,rb​]=rc​[Jaadj​]cb​.
(18)

This has exactly the form of the definition (4), with three operators and a valid set of 3×33\times33×3 representation matrices. But the matrices are the adjoint ones, not the standard spin-1 ones. For instance,

J3adj=[0−i0i00000]is notJ3(1)=[10000000−1].J_3^{\mathrm{adj}}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-i&0\\ i&0&0\\ 0&0&0\end{bmatrix} \quad\text{is not}\quad J_3^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&-1\end{bmatrix}.J3adj​=​0i0​−i00​000​​is notJ3(1)​=​100​000​00−1​​.
(19)

The two are equivalent: both are three-dimensional irreps of SU(2),SU(2)\text{,}SU(2), so they’re the same representation written in different bases. So there’s a similarity transformation SSS with

S Jaadj S−1=Ja(1).S\,J_a^{\mathrm{adj}}\,S^{-1} = J_a^{(1)}.SJaadj​S−1=Ja(1)​.
(20)

So r\vec rr is a spin-1 tensor operator written in the wrong basis. The next three sections show how to change basis.

5Converting to standard form

Suppose a set of operators Ωx,\Omega_x\text{,}Ωx​, for x=1,…,2s+1,x=1,\dots,2s+1\text{,}x=1,…,2s+1, satisfies

[Ja,Ωx]=Ωy[Ja(D)]yx,[J_a,\Omega_x] = \Omega_y\big[J_a^{(D)}\big]_{yx},[Ja​,Ωx​]=Ωy​[Ja(D)​]yx​,
(21)

where DDD is some representation equivalent to spin s,s\text{,}s, so that S Ja(D)S−1=Ja(s)S\,J_a^{(D)}S^{-1}=J_a^{(s)}SJa(D)​S−1=Ja(s)​ for some invertible S.S\text{.}S. Here’s the recipe. Define

Ols≡Ωy[S−1]yl,O^s_l \equiv \Omega_y\big[S^{-1}\big]_{yl},Ols​≡Ωy​[S−1]yl​,
(22)

so that OlsO^s_lOls​ is the combination of the Ω\OmegaΩ’s whose coefficients are the lllth column of S−1.S^{-1}\text{.}S−1. Then, inserting δku=[S−1]ke[S]eu,\delta_{ku}=[S^{-1}]_{ke}[S]_{eu}\text{,}δku​=[S−1]ke​[S]eu​,

[Ja,Ols]=[S−1]yl [Ja,Ωy]=[S−1]yl Ωk[Ja(D)]ky=[S−1]yl Ωk[S−1]ke[S]eu[Ja(D)]uy=(Ωk[S−1]ke)([S]eu[Ja(D)]uy[S−1]yl)=Oes [Ja(s)]el.\begin{aligned} {[J_a,O^s_l]} &= \big[S^{-1}\big]_{yl}\,[J_a,\Omega_y] = \big[S^{-1}\big]_{yl}\,\Omega_k\big[J_a^{(D)}\big]_{ky}\\ &= \big[S^{-1}\big]_{yl}\,\Omega_k\big[S^{-1}\big]_{ke}\big[S\big]_{eu}\big[J_a^{(D)}\big]_{uy}\\ &= \Big(\Omega_k\big[S^{-1}\big]_{ke}\Big)\Big(\big[S\big]_{eu}\big[J_a^{(D)}\big]_{uy}\big[S^{-1}\big]_{yl}\Big)\\ &= O^s_e\,\big[J_a^{(s)}\big]_{el}. \end{aligned}[Ja​,Ols​]​=[S−1]yl​[Ja​,Ωy​]=[S−1]yl​Ωk​[Ja(D)​]ky​=[S−1]yl​Ωk​[S−1]ke​[S]eu​[Ja(D)​]uy​=(Ωk​[S−1]ke​)([S]eu​[Ja(D)​]uy​[S−1]yl​)=Oes​[Ja(s)​]el​.​
(23)

So the OlsO^s_lOls​ form a spin-sss tensor operator in standard form. There are two ways to use this: we can avoid computing SSS at all, by building the OlsO^s_lOls​ with the ladder relations (Section 6), or we can compute SSS explicitly (Section 7).

6The ladder route

Suppose DDD is irreducible and sss is an integer. By the recipe, a standard-form set OlsO^s_lOls​ exists, and its O0sO^s_0O0s​ commutes with J3.J_3\text{.}J3​. The Ω\OmegaΩ’s are linearly independent: the coefficient vectors ccc with cyΩy=0c_y\Omega_y=0cy​Ωy​=0 form a DDD-invariant subspace (commuting JaJ_aJa​ through cyΩy=0c_y\Omega_y=0cy​Ωy​=0 gives Ωx[Ja(D)c]x=0),\Omega_x\big[J_a^{(D)}c\big]_x=0\text{),}Ωx​[Ja(D)​c]x​=0), so by irreducibility it’s {0},\{0\}\text{,}{0}, unless all the Ω\OmegaΩ’s vanish. And in an irrep the weight 0 occurs exactly once, so every combination of the Ω\OmegaΩ’s that commutes with J3J_3J3​ is a multiple of O0s.O^s_0\text{.}O0s​. The definition is linear in O,O\text{,}O, so its overall normalization is ours to choose. That gives a two-step recipe:

  • find the combination of Ω\OmegaΩ’s that commutes with J3,J_3\text{,}J3​, and call it O0s;O^s_0\text{;}O0s​;
  • generate the rest from the ladder relations, Ol±1s=[J±,Ols]/Cs,l±.O^s_{l\pm1}=[J^\pm,O^s_l]/C^\pm_{s,l}\text{.}Ol±1s​=[J±,Ols​]/Cs,l±​.

(For half-integer sss there’s no weight 0. Start instead from the combination of weight s,s\text{,}s, which is annihilated by [J+, ⋅ ],[J^+,\,\cdot\,]\text{,}[J+,⋅], and lower.)

Example (r\vec rr as a spin-1 tensor operator): Put r\vec rr into standard form by the ladder route.

Solution: With J3=r1p2−r2p1,J_3=r_1p_2-r_2p_1\text{,}J3​=r1​p2​−r2​p1​, we have [J3,r3]=0,[J_3,r_3]=0\text{,}[J3​,r3​]=0, while [J3,r1]=ir2[J_3,r_1]=ir_2[J3​,r1​]=ir2​ and [J3,r2]=−ir1.[J_3,r_2]=-ir_1\text{.}[J3​,r2​]=−ir1​. So up to normalization, r3r_3r3​ is the only combination that commutes with J3:J_3\text{:}J3​:

r~0=r3.\tilde r_0 = r_3 .r~0​=r3​.
(24)

From [Ja,rb]=iεabcrc,[J_a,r_b]=i\varepsilon_{abc}r_c\text{,}[Ja​,rb​]=iεabc​rc​, we have [J1,r3]=−ir2[J_1,r_3]=-ir_2[J1​,r3​]=−ir2​ and [J2,r3]=ir1.[J_2,r_3]=ir_1\text{.}[J2​,r3​]=ir1​. So

[J+,r~0]=12[J1,r3]+i2[J2,r3]=12(−ir2)+i2(ir1)=−12(r1+ir2),[J−,r~0]=12[J1,r3]−i2[J2,r3]=12(−ir2)−i2(ir1)=12(r1−ir2).\begin{aligned} {[J^+,\tilde r_0]} &= \tfrac1{\sqrt2}[J_1,r_3] + \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}[J_2,r_3] = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}(-ir_2) + \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}(ir_1)\\ &= -\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(r_1+ir_2),\\[4pt] {[J^-,\tilde r_0]} &= \tfrac1{\sqrt2}[J_1,r_3] - \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}[J_2,r_3] = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}(-ir_2) - \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}(ir_1)\\ &= \tfrac1{\sqrt2}(r_1-ir_2). \end{aligned}[J+,r~0​][J−,r~0​]​=2​1​[J1​,r3​]+2​i​[J2​,r3​]=2​1​(−ir2​)+2​i​(ir1​)=−2​1​(r1​+ir2​),=2​1​[J1​,r3​]−2​i​[J2​,r3​]=2​1​(−ir2​)−2​i​(ir1​)=2​1​(r1​−ir2​).​
(25)

Since C1,0±=121⋅2=1,C^\pm_{1,0}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\sqrt{1\cdot2}=1\text{,}C1,0±​=2​1​1⋅2​=1, these are r~±1\tilde r_{\pm1}r~±1​ directly:

Remark: Starting in the copy where spins 1 and 2 form a singlet, S(2) ⁣⋅S(3)\vec S^{(2)}\!\cdot\vec S^{(3)}S(2)⋅S(3) lands us entirely in the copy where they form a triplet. Problem 1 finds the whole 2×22\times22×2 matrix kαβk_{\alpha\beta}kαβ​ and explains what it’s telling us. ♣\clubsuit♣

12kαβk_{\alpha\beta}kαβ​ is independent of MMM

Apply J−J^-J− to eq. (41). On the left, J−∣J,M~⟩=CJ,M−∣J,M−1~⟩.J^-\tket{J}{M}=C^-_{J,M}\tket{J}{M-1}\text{.}J−∣J,M​⟩=CJ,M−​∣J,M−1​⟩. On the right, J−J^-J− acts on every copy with the same coefficient, and doesn’t change β:\beta\text{:}β:

CJ,M−∣J,M−1~⟩=CJ,M−∑βkαβ(M)∣J,M−1,β⟩.C^-_{J,M}\tket{J}{M-1} = C^-_{J,M}\sum_\beta k^{(M)}_{\alpha\beta}\ket{J,M-1,\beta}.CJ,M−​∣J,M−1​⟩=CJ,M−​β∑​kαβ(M)​∣J,M−1,β⟩.
(44)

Compare this with ∣J,M−1~⟩=∑βkαβ(M−1)∣J,M−1,β⟩.\tket{J}{M-1}=\sum_\beta k^{(M-1)}_{\alpha\beta}\ket{J,M-1,\beta}\text{.}∣J,M−1​⟩=∑β​kαβ(M−1)​∣J,M−1,β⟩. Since CJ,M−≠0C^-_{J,M}\neq0CJ,M−​=0 for M>−J,M>-J\text{,}M>−J, and the ∣J,M−1,β⟩\ket{J,M-1,\beta}∣J,M−1,β⟩ are linearly independent,

kαβ(M−1)=kαβ(M),k^{(M-1)}_{\alpha\beta}=k^{(M)}_{\alpha\beta},kαβ(M−1)​=kαβ(M)​,
(45)

so kαβk_{\alpha\beta}kαβ​ is independent of M.M\text{.}M. It doesn’t depend on any single lll either, since ∣J,M~⟩\tket{J}{M}∣J,M​⟩ is a sum over all l.l\text{.}l. What kαβk_{\alpha\beta}kαβ​ does depend on is the irrep ∣j,α⟩\ket{j,\alpha}∣j,α⟩ and the operator OsO^sOs that we started the construction from; the tower JJJ of s⊗js\otimes js⊗j that we’re in; and the copy β\betaβ of JJJ that we land on. The notation kαβk_{\alpha\beta}kαβ​ shows only α\alphaα and β,\beta\text{,}β, and leaves the dependence on J,J\text{,}J, jjj and OsO^sOs implicit.

13Inverting the construction

In the product space the coupled basis is complete, and only M=l+mM=l+mM=l+m contributes, so

∣s,l⟩∣j,m⟩=∑J=∣j−s∣j+s∣J,l+m⟩ ⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩.\ket{s,l}\ket{j,m} = \sum_{J=|j-s|}^{j+s} \ket{J,l+m}\,\GC{l}{m}{J}{l+m}.∣s,l⟩∣j,m⟩=J=∣j−s∣∑j+s​∣J,l+m⟩⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩.
(46)

Apply Φα\Phi_\alphaΦα​ to both sides, and then expand each ∣J,l+m~⟩\tket{J}{l+m}∣J,l+m​⟩ with eq. (41):

Ols∣j,m,α⟩=∑J=∣j−s∣j+s⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩ ∣J,l+m~⟩=∑J=∣j−s∣j+s∑β⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩  kαβ ∣J,l+m,β⟩.\begin{aligned} O^s_l\ket{j,m,\alpha} &= \sum_{J=|j-s|}^{j+s} \GC{l}{m}{J}{l+m}\,\tket{J}{l+m}\\ &= \sum_{J=|j-s|}^{j+s}\sum_{\beta} \GC{l}{m}{J}{l+m}\;k_{\alpha\beta}\,\ket{J,l+m,\beta}. \end{aligned}Ols​∣j,m,α⟩​=J=∣j−s∣∑j+s​⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩∣J,l+m​⟩=J=∣j−s∣∑j+s​β∑​⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩kαβ​∣J,l+m,β⟩.​
(47)

Now project onto ⟨J′,M′,β′∣,\bra{J',M',\beta'}\text{,}⟨J′,M′,β′∣, using ⟨J′,M′,β′∣J,M,β⟩=δJ′JδM′Mδβ′β.\braket{J',M',\beta'}{J,M,\beta}=\delta_{J'J}\delta_{M'M}\delta_{\beta'\beta}\text{.}⟨J′,M′,β′∣J,M,β⟩=δJ′J​δM′M​δβ′β​. (The inner sum over β\betaβ runs over the copies of the JJJ in the outer sum.) Dropping the primes,

⟨J,M′,β∣Ols∣j,m,α⟩=δM′, l+m  kαβ  ⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩\bra{J,M',\beta}O^s_l\ket{j,m,\alpha} = \delta_{M',\,l+m}\;k_{\alpha\beta}\;\GC{l}{m}{J}{l+m}⟨J,M′,β∣Ols​∣j,m,α⟩=δM′,l+m​kαβ​⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩
(48)

for ∣j−s∣≤J≤j+s,|j-s|\le J\le j+s\text{,}∣j−s∣≤J≤j+s, and the matrix element vanishes for JJJ outside this range.

14The Wigner–Eckart theorem

To make the dependence of kαβk_{\alpha\beta}kαβ​ explicit, write it as the reduced matrix element

kαβ≡⟨J,β∥Os∥j,α⟩.k_{\alpha\beta}\equiv\langle J,\beta\Vert O^s\Vert j,\alpha\rangle .kαβ​≡⟨J,β∥Os∥j,α⟩.
(49)

Then we have

  ⟨J,l+m,β∣ Ols ∣j,m,α⟩=⟨J,β∥Os∥j,α⟩  ⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩  \boxed{\;\bra{J,l+m,\beta}\,O^s_l\,\ket{j,m,\alpha} = \langle J,\beta\Vert O^s\Vert j,\alpha\rangle\;\GC{l}{m}{J}{l+m}\;}⟨J,l+m,β∣Ols​∣j,m,α⟩=⟨J,β∥Os∥j,α⟩⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩​
(50)

This is the Wigner–Eckart theorem. All matrix elements ⟨J,M′,β∣Ols∣j,m,α⟩\bra{J,M',\beta}O^s_l\ket{j,m,\alpha}⟨J,M′,β∣Ols​∣j,m,α⟩ with M′≠l+m,M'\neq l+m\text{,}M′=l+m, or with JJJ outside ∣j−s∣≤J≤j+s,|j-s|\le J\le j+s\text{,}∣j−s∣≤J≤j+s, vanish. The left side is some, possibly nasty, integral. The right side splits it into a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient, which is pure group theory and carries all of the lll and mmm dependence, and a single number that knows nothing about lll or m.m\text{.}m. Equivalently, for any lll and mmm whose Clebsch–Gordan coefficient is nonzero,

⟨J,β∥Os∥j,α⟩=⟨J,l+m,β∣Ols∣j,m,α⟩⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩,\langle J,\beta\Vert O^s\Vert j,\alpha\rangle = \frac{\bra{J,l+m,\beta}O^s_l\ket{j,m,\alpha}}{\GC{l}{m}{J}{l+m}},⟨J,β∥Os∥j,α⟩=⟨J,l+m∣s,j;l,m⟩⟨J,l+m,β∣Ols​∣j,m,α⟩​,
(51)

and the ratio is the same for every such choice.

That’s what makes the theorem useful. Evaluate the left side once, for one convenient l,ml,ml,m with a nonzero Clebsch–Gordan coefficient. Look up that coefficient and divide, to get the reduced matrix element. Then look up the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients for all the other lll and m,m\text{,}m, and the corresponding matrix elements follow practically for free.

Said Wigner, surveying the mazeOf integrals, set in a haze:“Every mmm and each lllIs a CG’s to tell;Only one number’s left to appraise.”

17Solutions

1. Recoupling by diagonalizing

Row α=1\alpha=1α=1 is the example: k11=0k_{11}=0k11​=0 and k12=34.k_{12}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\text{.}k12​=43​​. For row α=2,\alpha=2\text{,}α=2, the same counting as in the example gives O00∣12,12,2⟩=34∣12,12,1⟩−12∣12,12,2⟩,O^0_0\ket{\tfrac12,\tfrac12,2}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\ket{\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1}-\tfrac12 \ket{\tfrac12,\tfrac12,2}\text{,}O00​∣21​,21​,2⟩=43​​∣21​,21​,1⟩−21​∣21​,21​,2⟩, so k21=34k_{21}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}k21​=43​​ and k22=−12.k_{22}=-\tfrac12\text{.}k22​=−21​. (That k21=k12k_{21}=k_{12}k21​=k12​ is no accident: O00O^0_0O00​ is Hermitian.) So

k=[03434−12].k = \begin{bmatrix}0 & \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\\[2pt] \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4} & -\tfrac12\end{bmatrix}.k=[043​​​43​​−21​​].
(53)

Its characteristic polynomial is μ2+12μ−316=(μ−14)(μ+34),\mu^2+\tfrac12\mu-\tfrac3{16}=(\mu-\tfrac14)(\mu+\tfrac34)\text{,}μ2+21​μ−163​=(μ−41​)(μ+43​), so the eigenvalues are 14\tfrac1441​ and −34.-\tfrac34\text{.}−43​. For μ=−34,\mu=-\tfrac34\text{,}μ=−43​, the eigenvector is (1,−3)/2,(1,-\sqrt3)/2\text{,}(1,−3​)/2, and the corresponding state is

12∣12,12,1⟩−32∣12,12,2⟩=−12(∣↑↑↓⟩−∣↑↓↑⟩),\tfrac12\ket{\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1}-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\ket{\tfrac12,\tfrac12,2} = -\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\big(\ket{\U\U\D}-\ket{\U\D\U}\big),21​∣21​,21​,1⟩−23​​∣21​,21​,2⟩=−2​1​(∣↑↑↓⟩−∣↑↓↑⟩),
(54)

which is particle 1 up, times the singlet of particles 2 and 3. The other eigenvector is orthogonal to it, so it’s particle 1 coupled to the triplet of particles 2 and 3.

Remark: This makes sense: S(2) ⁣⋅S(3)=12[(S(2)+S(3))2−S(2)2−S(3)2]=12[s23(s23+1)−32],\vec S^{(2)}\!\cdot\vec S^{(3)}=\tfrac12\big[(\vec S^{(2)}+\vec S^{(3)})^2-\vec S^{(2)2}- \vec S^{(3)2}\big]=\tfrac12\big[s_{23}(s_{23}+1)-\tfrac32\big]\text{,}S(2)⋅S(3)=21​[(S(2)+S(3))2−S(2)2−S(3)2]=21​[s23​(s23​+1)−23​], which is 14\tfrac1441​ for s23=1s_{23}=1s23​=1 and −34-\tfrac34−43​ for s23=0.s_{23}=0\text{.}s23​=0. The two copies of spin 12\tfrac1221​ can be labeled by coupling particles 1 and 2 first, or 2 and 3 first, and the matrix of reduced matrix elements of S(2) ⁣⋅S(3)\vec S^{(2)}\!\cdot\vec S^{(3)}S(2)⋅S(3) is exactly what translates between the two labelings. ♣\clubsuit♣

2. Scalar operators

For s=0s=0s=0 the spin-0 “matrices” are 1×11\times11×1 zeros, so the definition just says [Ja,O00]=0.[J_a,O^0_0]=0\text{.}[Ja​,O00​]=0. And 0⊗j=j:0\otimes j=j\text{:}0⊗j=j: the only tower is J=j,J=j\text{,}J=j, with ∣J,M⟩=∣0,0⟩∣j,M⟩,\ket{J,M}=\ket{0,0} \ket{j,M}\text{,}∣J,M⟩=∣0,0⟩∣j,M⟩, so the Clebsch–Gordan coefficient is δMm.\delta_{Mm}\text{.}δMm​. So the theorem reads

⟨J,M,β∣O00∣j,m,α⟩=δJj δMm ⟨j,β∥O0∥j,α⟩.\bra{J,M,\beta}O^0_0\ket{j,m,\alpha} = \delta_{Jj}\,\delta_{Mm}\,\langle j,\beta\Vert O^0\Vert j,\alpha\rangle .⟨J,M,β∣O00​∣j,m,α⟩=δJj​δMm​⟨j,β∥O0∥j,α⟩.
(55)

A scalar can’t change jjj or m,m\text{,}m, and its matrix elements are the same for every m.m\text{.}m. But it can move a state from one copy of jjj to another, as S(2) ⁣⋅S(3)\vec S^{(2)}\!\cdot\vec S^{(3)}S(2)⋅S(3) does in the example of Section 11.

J\vec JJ itself satisfies [Ja,Jb]=iεabcJc,[J_a,J_b]=i\varepsilon_{abc}J_c\text{,}[Ja​,Jb​]=iεabc​Jc​, the same relation as [Ja,rb]=iεabcrc,[J_a,r_b]=i\varepsilon_{abc}r_c\text{,}[Ja​,rb​]=iεabc​rc​, so its spherical components J~±1=∓J±\tilde J_{\pm1}=\mp J^\pmJ~±1​=∓J± and J~0=J3\tilde J_0=J_3J~0​=J3​ form a spin-1 tensor operator. By the theorem, within the copy α,\alpha\text{,}α,

⟨j,m′,α∣V~l∣j,m,α⟩=kV ⟨j,m′∣1,j;l,m⟩,⟨j,m′,α∣J~l∣j,m,α⟩=kJ ⟨j,m′∣1,j;l,m⟩,\begin{aligned} \bra{j,m',\alpha}\tilde V_l\ket{j,m,\alpha} &= k_V\,\langle j,m'\vert 1,j;l,m\rangle,\\ \bra{j,m',\alpha}\tilde J_l\ket{j,m,\alpha} &= k_J\,\langle j,m'\vert 1,j;l,m\rangle, \end{aligned}⟨j,m′,α∣V~l​∣j,m,α⟩⟨j,m′,α∣J~l​∣j,m,α⟩​=kV​⟨j,m′∣1,j;l,m⟩,=kJ​⟨j,m′∣1,j;l,m⟩,​
(56)

with kJ≠0k_J\neq0kJ​=0 for j>0j>0j>0 (for instance, ⟨j,j,α∣J3∣j,j,α⟩=j).\bra{j,j,\alpha}J_3\ket{j,j,\alpha}=j\text{).}⟨j,j,α∣J3​∣j,j,α⟩=j). So every matrix element of V~l\tilde V_lV~l​ is c≡kV/kJc\equiv k_V/k_Jc≡kV​/kJ​ times the corresponding one of J~l,\tilde J_l\text{,}J~l​, and since the Cartesian components are fixed combinations of the spherical ones, the same holds for VaV_aVa​ and Ja.J_a\text{.}Ja​. To find c,c\text{,}c, use the fact that JaJ_aJa​ never leaves the copy α,\alpha\text{,}α, so that in J⋅V=JaVa\vec J\cdot\vec V=J_aV_aJ⋅V=Ja​Va​ the intermediate states all lie in it:

⟨j,m,α∣JaVa∣j,m,α⟩=∑m′⟨j,m,α∣Ja∣j,m′,α⟩⟨j,m′,α∣Va∣j,m,α⟩=c ⟨j,m,α∣J 2∣j,m,α⟩=c j(j+1).\begin{aligned} &\bra{j,m,\alpha}J_aV_a\ket{j,m,\alpha}\\ &\qquad= \sum_{m'}\bra{j,m,\alpha}J_a\ket{j,m',\alpha}\bra{j,m',\alpha}V_a\ket{j,m,\alpha}\\ &\qquad= c\,\bra{j,m,\alpha}\vec J^{\,2}\ket{j,m,\alpha} = c\,j(j+1). \end{aligned}​⟨j,m,α∣Ja​Va​∣j,m,α⟩=m′∑​⟨j,m,α∣Ja​∣j,m′,α⟩⟨j,m′,α∣Va​∣j,m,α⟩=c⟨j,m,α∣J2∣j,m,α⟩=cj(j+1).​
(57)

So c=⟨J⋅V⟩/j(j+1),c=\langle\vec J\cdot\vec V\rangle/j(j+1)\text{,}c=⟨J⋅V⟩/j(j+1), which is the result.
